blocks.title: The Operating System Behind Almost Everything
blocks.subtitle: Kernel, shell, files and the open-source model

blocks.text:
Linux runs phones, web servers, routers, televisions, spacecraft and every one of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers. Most people use it daily without knowing.

It began as one student's hobby and grew into the largest collaborative software project ever undertaken. This story explains what Linux is, how it is organised and why it spread so far.

blocks.heading: Kernel and user space
blocks.text: The **kernel** is the core program that controls the hardware. It schedules processes, manages memory, runs device drivers and enforces permissions. Everything else, from the shell to the web browser, runs in **user space** and asks the kernel for services through system calls. A **distribution** packages the kernel with the tools and applications that make a complete system.

steps.text: **Firmware.** On power-up, UEFI or BIOS firmware tests the hardware and finds a device to boot from.
**Bootloader.** A bootloader such as GRUB loads the kernel and an initial file system into memory.
**Kernel.** The kernel initialises memory, drivers and the root file system, then starts the first process.
**Init system.** The init system, commonly systemd, starts services and finally offers a login.

blocks.heading: Everything is a file
blocks.text: Unix-like systems present devices, pipes and even kernel information through the same interface as ordinary files. Small programs that each do one job can therefore be chained together, the output of one feeding the next. This design, and the plain-text configuration that goes with it, is why Linux is so easy to automate.

items.title: File system hierarchy
items.text: A single tree starting at /, with standard places such as /etc, /home and /var.

items.title: Process
items.text: A running program with its own memory and an identifying number.

items.title: Permissions
items.text: Read, write and execute rights for the owner, a group and everyone else.

items.title: Package manager

blocks.heading: Where the difficulties lie
blocks.text: Choice brings fragmentation: hundreds of distributions differ in packaging and defaults. Hardware support depends on makers releasing drivers or documentation. And because so much critical infrastructure depends on components maintained by small volunteer teams, funding and securing that shared code has become a serious concern.

blocks.question: What is the role of the kernel?
options: It manages hardware and resources for all other programs
blocks.explanation: The kernel schedules processes, manages memory and controls devices on behalf of user programs.

blocks.question: A file's permissions are 'rwxr-x---'. Who can read it?
options: The owner and members of the file's group
blocks.explanation: The three triplets are owner (rwx), group (r-x) and others (---).

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Distribution**: a packaged Linux system such as Debian, Ubuntu or Fedora. **Root**: the administrator account, and also the top directory /. **Daemon**: a background service. **System call**: a request from a program to the kernel. **Open source**: software whose source may be read, changed and shared.
